Pilot supplies

What a student pilot actually needs, and roughly in the order you will need it.

  1. Logbook. Paper is fine; an electronic logbook is fine too. Bring it to every lesson.
  2. Headset. Borrow one for the first few flights, then buy one you can wear for three hours. Passive noise reduction is enough to start.
  3. The free FAA handbooks (see the reading list below). Download the PDFs before you spend money on anything printed.
  4. Kneeboard with a pad and a pen that works upside down.
  5. Charts. The San Francisco sectional and the Chart Supplement, on paper or in an EFB app on a tablet. We will talk about which before you buy an iPad.
  6. Fuel tester and a flashlight with a red or dim setting for night flights.
  7. E6B and plotter. A mechanical E6B teaches you what the app is doing; buy the cheap one.
  8. Pilot Operating Handbook for the airplane you fly. Read the normal and emergency procedures before your third lesson.
  9. Later: a view-limiting device for instrument training, and a pulse oximeter for mountain flying.

Documents to carry once you have them: your medical certificate and student pilot certificate, and your logbook with current endorsements.

Checklists

Before your first solo

  • Medical certificate and student pilot certificate in hand.
  • Pre-solo knowledge test completed and reviewed with me (§61.87(b)).
  • Pre-solo flight training in the maneuvers and procedures of §61.87(d), logged.
  • Logbook endorsements: aeronautical knowledge, flight proficiency, and the 90-day solo endorsement for the make and model.
  • Student pilot certificate endorsement for the make and model.
  • You can explain, without notes, what you would do after an engine failure on climb-out, and where you would go if the tower's radio failed.

What to bring to your checkride

  • Government photo ID; student pilot certificate; medical certificate.
  • Logbook with every required endorsement (§61.103, §61.105, §61.107, §61.109, and the §61.39 practical-test endorsement), with the aeronautical experience totalled and easy to find.
  • Knowledge test report, with any missed subject areas reviewed and endorsed.
  • IACRA application completed and signed by me, and your FTN.
  • The examiner's fee, in the form the examiner asks for.
  • Aircraft documents: airworthiness certificate, registration, operating limitations or POH, weight and balance.
  • Maintenance records showing the annual inspection, the transponder and altimeter/static checks, the ELT, and compliance with airworthiness directives.
  • Your cross-country plan for the route the examiner assigned, with weight and balance, performance calculations, a weather briefing and NOTAMs.
  • Current charts or EFB, plotter, E6B, headset, view-limiting device.
  • A copy of the ACS, and water and a snack. It is a long day.

Reading lists

Student and Private Pilot

All of the FAA titles are free from the FAA handbooks page.

  • Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (PHAK) — the textbook.
  • Airplane Flying Handbook (AFH) — how each maneuver is flown.
  • Aviation Weather Handbook — replaces the old AC 00-6 and AC 00-45.
  • Risk Management Handbook — how the FAA wants you to think about decisions.
  • Private Pilot – Airplane Airman Certification Standards — what the checkride tests, and the study guide for the oral exam.
  • FAR/AIM — Part 61 and Part 91 online, plus the Aeronautical Information Manual. A printed FAR/AIM is worth owning.
  • AC 90-66, Non-Towered Airport Flight Operations — Advisory Circulars.
  • The POH of the airplane you fly.
  • Aeronautical Chart Users' Guide — online.

Instrument rating

  • Instrument Flying Handbook and Instrument Procedures Handbook — free from the FAA.
  • Instrument Rating – Airplane ACS.
  • AIM Chapter 5 (Air Traffic Procedures), read twice.
  • The Garmin G1000 Cockpit Reference Guide and Pilot's Guide for the airplane you fly — free from Garmin's support site.
  • Terminal procedures for the approaches we fly, current cycle.

Garmin G1000

  • Garmin's Pilot's Guide and Cockpit Reference Guide for your airframe.
  • Garmin's own G1000 training videos, and the free G1000 PC trainer if it is available for your airplane.
  • TBDother G1000 material

Official references

  • eCFR Title 14, Part 61 — certification of pilots and instructors.
  • eCFR Title 14, Part 91 — general operating and flight rules.
  • Aeronautical Information Manual.
  • Airman Certification Standards.
  • FAA aviation handbooks and manuals.
  • Advisory Circulars.
  • Digital charts and the Chart Supplement.
  • Aviation Weather Center and 1800wxbrief for briefings.
  • NOTAM search.
  • IACRA — certificate applications. MedXPress — medical applications.
  • PSI — scheduling knowledge tests.
  • FAASafety.gov — WINGS proficiency program and free courses.
  • AirNav and SkyVector — airport information and planning.
  • West Valley Flying Club.
